summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis. The age of consent is set at 14 years equally regardless of gender and sexual orientation, with sex below that age treated as statutory rape.

Statutory protection at state level is explicit. The amended Anti-Discrimination Law adopted in 2016 covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics in the terminology used locally; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination had covered sexual orientation and gender expression but omitted gender identity as originally intended. The Sarajevo Open Centre presented the 2016 amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality after public consultations held in autumn 2015.

Hate-crime sentencing enhancement exists at entity level. In April 2016 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code to name sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances, published 15 June 2016; Republika Srpska and Brčko District run their own separate regimes with similar provisions. The Federation's adoption followed sustained coalition advocacy, confirmed by Sarajevo Open Centre coordinator Vladana Vasić.

Public expression has repeatedly drawn violence. The Queer Sarajevo Festival in 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats, leaving eight people including a policeman injured; in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that authorities had failed to protect participants' freedom of assembly. Organised anti-LGBT violence has occurred even with prior police coordination: staff of the Sarajevo Open Centre said they had arranged security with police about three weeks before the February 2014 attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers, and Human Rights Watch's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of the attackers. The first Pride march in Bosnia and Herzegovina was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers. In March 2023 police cancelled LGBTQ film screenings in Banja Luka over security concerns, and activists were chased and attacked afterwards.

The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, published 13 June 2024, records a number of negative events over the past year with significant impact and describes the long-visible worsening trend as becoming increasingly evident.

Legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice. The Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on completed medical transition, and Balkan Diskurs reported on 25 October 2024 that these constraints are described as discriminatory and degrading; legal gender change is available only after sex reassignment surgery and other medical treatments. This pathway is a resident-facing burden rather than a border issue, but it shapes what documents a trans person can present.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples at national or subnational level. The Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couple households are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples. On 19 October 2018 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a request to legalise civil unions; a working group was established in January 2020 but its start was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Healthcare and social climate carry documented risk. A 2017 PLOS ONE qualitative study documents the stigma and discrimination men who have sex with men experience from healthcare professionals and the general community. A 2015 survey found 48% of Bosnians would try to 'cure' their child if the child came out as gay and 16% would stop communicating with that child; the same survey found 19% supported granting same-sex couples some marriage-associated rights, and a 2017 Pew poll found 13% support for same-sex marriage with 84% opposed. A 2021 study found the 2019 Sarajevo Pride parade increased support for LGBT activism only in Sarajevo, not nationwide.

The legal framework is split across two entities plus Brčko District, so protections and enforcement vary by where a visitor is standing. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska and Brčko District each maintain their own criminal and family codes, and hate-crime provisions naming sexual orientation and gender identity were adopted separately rather than uniformly.

Public visibility carries a documented violence risk that is not confined to counter-protest. The 2008 Queer Sarajevo Festival attack and the March 2023 Banja Luka incidents show that cultural events and screenings can be targeted even where police are aware of them; the 2014 attack on Pride organisers followed advance security coordination with police.

Public opinion polling from 2015 and 2017 indicates substantial social hostility to LGBT rights, with 84% opposed to same-sex marriage in the 2017 Pew poll. A 2021 study found the 2019 Pride parade shifted attitudes only in Sarajevo, suggesting that visibility gains do not generalise across the country.

The 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibited discrimination on sexual orientation and included gender expression but omitted gender identity as originally intended; the 2016 amendment closed that gap at state level. outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the Federation's 2018 civil-union request and the January 2020 working group is unresolved in the source inventory; no source confirms whether the working group has since convened or produced a draft.

Whether Republika Srpska and Brčko District hate-crime provisions have produced comparable prosecutions to the Federation's is not sourced here; enforcement rates by entity remain unverified.

The practical operation of the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan after the October 2024 reporting is not sourced; whether any cases have been approved without completed surgery is unresolved.

Post-2024 incident data beyond the Pink Report 2024's summary of a worsening trend is not available in this inventory, so the current frequency of anti-LGBT violence is not established.
